questions.q: What are the four parts of the standard architecture-principle template used in this lesson?
options: Name, statement, rationale, implications
Title, author, date, version
Budget, timeline, owner, status
Problem, solution, cost, benefit
questions.explain: The lesson's template has four parts: name, statement, rationale, and implications.

questions.q: What does the 'single source of truth' principle require?
options: Exactly one authoritative definition and location for a given business concept
Every team maintains its own independent definition of each concept
Data must be stored in exactly one physical database with no replication ever
Only the central IT team may ever look at the data
questions.explain: The principle is about one authoritative definition per concept, even if it's physically replicated elsewhere.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'automate enforcement, don't rely on memory' matters?
options: A rule that depends on someone remembering to apply it will eventually be broken by accident at scale
Automation is always cheaper than hiring people
Manual review is illegal under most data regulations
Automated systems never make mistakes
questions.explain: The lesson's rationale is about manual enforcement silently degrading and not scaling — not cost or legality.

questions.q: What does the 'design for loose coupling' principle enable, per the lesson?
options: Federated and mesh-style operating models become technically possible
It eliminates the need for any metadata layer
It guarantees a single central system will always be sufficient
It removes the need for any integration layer at all
questions.explain: The lesson states loose coupling, connecting through defined interfaces, is what makes federated and mesh-style models technically possible.

questions.q: In the worked example, what is the 'implications' part of the Automate Enforcement principle?
options: New policies must be expressible as code, or flagged as a known gap
All existing policies must be deleted immediately
No new policy may ever be written again
Only the CEO may approve new policies
questions.explain: The worked example's implications state that new policies need to be expressible as code (or explicitly flagged as not-yet-automatable).
